content.passage:
### The United Kingdom
There are four separate countries in the United Kingdom. These are the two kingdoms of England and Scotland, the principality of Wales and the province of Northern Ireland. Each country has its own capital. Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland, Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland and Cardiff is the capital of Wales. London is the capital of England and also of the UK.

### Language
There are three main languages in the UK. English is an official language everywhere, but Welsh is the second official language in Wales. There are radio and TV programmes in Welsh and it is used on road signs and official documents. Gaelic is spoken in parts of Scotland.

### History
The country has been called the United Kingdom only since the beginning of the 19th century. Before that it was called Britain or Great Britain. Wales was united with England in 1282. In 1603 the king of Scotland became the king of all three countries. Ireland became part of the UK in 1801. Southern Ireland became an independent republic in 1921.

### System of government
The United Kingdom is a parliamentary monarchy. This means that the monarch, the king or queen, is the Head of State but has no real power. The king or queen 'reigns', but does not 'rule'. The country is ruled or governed by a parliament. In 1649, after a long Civil War, Britain became a republic. It had no king or queen, but was ruled by a kind of president. It became a monarchy again in 1660.

### The Union Jack
The flag of the United Kingdom, the Union Jack, consists of the flags of England, Scotland and Northern Ireland. It is a symbol of the unity of the country.

### From Empire to Commonwealth
In 1945 the UK was still the head of the British Empire, which covered a quarter of the world's surface. A quarter of the population of the world was governed from London. Most of the countries of the Empire are now independent, but they have stayed members of a kind of international club called the Commonwealth.

content.passage:
Queen Victoria's life covers most of the 19th century. She became Queen of the United Kingdom in 1837 when she was only 18 years old. Three years later, she married Albert, a German prince. They had nine children. Albert died in 1861. After his death, Victoria wore black clothes for the rest of her life. She herself died in 1901 at the age of 81 and is the longest reigning British monarch.

People's daily life changed greatly during Victoria's reign. Industry became more important than agriculture and many people moved from the country to towns to work in the new factories. At first the towns were dirty and unhealthy, but slowly things improved. New sewers took away the waste water from people's homes and houses were built with gardens. Big towns had libraries, art galleries and parks. In 1837, only rich people went to school, but by 1901 education was free for everybody up to the age of twelve. Railways were built in every part of the kingdom. People became richer and were able to buy more goods. Hundreds of new shops opened. Covered shopping centres, called arcades, were built in the large towns. Towards the end of the century, large department stores opened. Shoppers could now buy nearly everything they wanted in one step.

The adjective 'Victorian' describes things typical of the time of the Queen's reign. Victorian buildings were often decorated with statues and carved stone. The architecture imitated the style of church buildings of five centuries earlier. Typical Victorian fashion in clothing was floor-length dresses for women and long black coats for men. Victorian values included hard work and strict discipline for children. The saying "children should be seen and not heard" comes from this time.

questions.question: Is Alan Cooper for or against the new supermarket?
Is Jenny Green for or against the new supermarket?
Is Sally Woodman for or against the factory closing?
Is Fred Mason for or against the factory closing?

content.transcript: Alan Cooper: I'm completely against the idea of another one. I'm a market-trader. Ten years ago there used to be a good market here in the town centre every day. There were stalls that used to sell everything from meat and fish to soap and light bulbs. Now we have a market once a week. Lots of shops have closed as well. The post office used to be a baker's and the new cafe is in a butcher's. It's all because of those supermarkets. They don't care about people. I don't have a car and I don't drive. Jenny Green: I can't wait for the new supermarket. I'm all for it. It's great to be able to get everything in one shop. It's so convenient. I don't have time to go around to different shops, carrying heavy shopping. I remember shopping in the market. It was very crowded and shopping took ages. They say that we'll soon be able to shop from home using a computer. I'm looking forward to that. Sally Woodman: Johnson's was an old-fashioned factory. It made things that other factories don't make anymore. It was also a dirty place to work. I'm in favour of it closing. This town needs new industries, like electronics. New factories are cleaner and places to work. I hope the new industries create lots of jobs for women. Fred Mason: I've worked at Johnson's since I was 16. I'm an engineer. I can't do anything else. So, I'm not in favour of it closing. I know that new industries are coming to the town but they're not going to take men from Johnson's. We're all going to have to move to another part of the country to get new jobs. I don't know what I'm going to do.

content.passage:
A new out-of-town supermarket is opening, and the old engineering factory is closing, causing mixed reactions among the residents. 

**Alan Cooper**, an elderly resident, is unhappy. 'The new supermarket is too far away, and I don't have a car,' he says. 'Many local shops, like the baker's and the butcher's, have already closed. It's a shame.'

**Jenny Green**, a busy working mother, has a different view. 'I'm looking forward to it! I don't have time to go to different shops. Buying everything I need in one place will be so convenient. They also say we'll soon be able to shop from home using a computer.'

**Sally Woodman** is optimistic about the factory closing. 'It's sad that 150 jobs will be lost, but the factory was old-fashioned. The town needs new industries like electronics. These new industries create jobs for women, which is great for the town's future.'

**Fred Mason**, who worked at the factory, is worried. 'I've worked in engineering my whole life. There are no jobs in these new industries for men like me. I don't know what I'm going to do. Maybe I'll have to dig gardens to earn money.'

content.passage:
The Tower of London is one of the oldest buildings in the United Kingdom. It stands on the bank of the River Thames in the middle of London. The central tower was built by King William the First in the 11th century to show the power of the King to the people of London. It was painted white in 1241 and since then has been called The White Tower. The outer walls were added in the 12th and 13th centuries.

The building has been used in many different ways. It was first a royal palace where the kings and queens could live safely. Later it was used as a prison for traitors - people who committed serious crimes against the king or country. Prisoners were brought into the tower from the river through a special gate, now called Traitor's Gate. Many prisoners were executed for their crimes. The executioner cut their heads off with an axe.

Nowadays the Tower of London is a museum. Apart from looking at the old building itself, visitors can see many interesting exhibits. The most famous exhibit is the Crown Jewels. This is a set of very valuable jewellery. It is a symbol of the power of the king or queen. The biggest piece is the crown itself, which is put in the head of a new king or queen at a special ceremony called a coronation. The largest diamond in the world, the Star of Africa, is set in another piece of jewellery.

Visitors will also notice that many ravens live in the gardens of the Tower. There is a superstition that the building will collapse and the monarchy will fall if these big black birds ever fly away. The feathers on the ravens' wings are cut to stop this happening.

The Prince, who later became King George the Fourth, bought it in 1785. It was made larger in the years 1801 and 1802. The next big changes happened between 1815 and 1823, when the Pavilion was rebuilt. The inside of the building was decorated in the beautiful Chinese style. The outside, as you can see, was decorated in the Indian style. After King George, his brother, King William, used the Pavilion. He died in 1837. His successor, Queen Victoria, visited Brighton but did not like the Pavilion. She said it was 'a strange, odd, Chinese-looking place, both inside and outside'. She sold it to the town of Brighton in 1850. The rooms you will see on this tour include the breakfast room, dining room, the library, a conservatory, the kitchen, and the music room. (Part 2) ... that was the main dining room with its rich decorations. Now, we are in the Great Kitchen. Stand here, please, ladies and gentlemen. You'll be able to see better. To your left by the wall are the cookers where food was boiled or fried and in front of them some tables where the food was prepared - the preparation tables. This is where meat and vegetables were chopped and sauces made and so on. When the food was cooked, it was put on the big table in front of you - the steam table. The table top is made of metal. Steam from boiling water came along pipes to the space under the top and this is how they kept the food hot before it went into the dining room. To your right is a big fire where the meat was cooked. And on the shelves on the wall in front of you are all the pans. Now if you look up, you will see that the room is very high and that there are a lot of windows. content.passage:
## An English tradition

**Presenter:** The police want to cancel this year's cheese rolling race. With me to talk about it are John Shepherd and Sergeant Lewis, a local policeman. John Shepherd wants the race to go ahead. Sergeant Lewis doesn't. Mr Shepherd, what is the cheese rolling race?

**John Shepherd:** We roll wheel-shaped cheeses down a hill and about 30 people run down after them and try to catch them.

**Presenter:** Do they ever catch the cheeses?

**John Shepherd:** Never. The winner is the first person to reach the bottom of the hill.

**Presenter:** And you want to stop this race, Sergeant Lewis. Why?

**Sergeant Lewis:** It's just too dangerous. Last year 35 people were injured, some of them people who had just come to watch. The people running down the hill fell and broke their legs or arms. Many were taken to hospital by helicopters and ambulances.

**Presenter:** How were the spectators injured?

**Sergeant Lewis:** These cheeses are heavy - about three kilos - and they go downhill very fast. Sometimes they bounce off the ground into the crowd and cause serious injuries. The race causes too much work for the emergency services. They have better things to do.

**John Shepherd:** I agree that it's dangerous, but nobody has ever been killed and it's very popular. Thousands of people come to watch the races. They've taken place for hundreds of years - some people say since the Romans were here 1,600 years ago - and we don't want to stop it now. It's a tradition.

**Presenter:** But if people are injured, it should be stopped, shouldn't it?

**John Shepherd:** They choose to take part. It's just a bit of fun. We live in a time when people aren't allowed to have fun or to do anything dangerous.

**Sergeant Lewis:** We don't want to stop people having fun. We just want to protect the spectators and prevent injuries. It must be organized better.

**John Shepherd:** We'll see what we can do for next year.

**Presenter:** Mr Shepherd, Sergeant Lewis, thank you.

content.passage:
### SCOTLAND
Scotland is the most northern country in the United Kingdom. Although part of the UK, Scotland still has its own legal and educational systems. It also competes independently in international sports, such as football and rugby. In fact, many Scots think that Scotland should become independent again.

### PHYSICAL
There are three main geographical areas in Scotland. The mountainous area in the north is called The Highlands. This area contains the highest mountain in the UK, Ben Nevis, which rises to 1,343 metres above sea level. There are several lochs (lakes) in this area, the best-known one being Loch Ness. A flat plain called The Lowlands crosses the centre of the country. Most of Scotland’s population of about 5,200,000 live here. The third part of Scotland, The Southern Uplands, is hilly. Scotland has many rivers. The Spey and Tay are famous for salmon fishing and the Clyde, which flows through Glasgow, used to be famous for ship-building.

### INCOME
In The Highlands, farming and fishing are the traditional sources of income. Scottish beef is world-famous and Scottish fish is exported to many countries. In the past twenty or thirty years, however, tourism has brought a lot of money into the area. Another important change was caused by the discovery of oil in the North Sea of Scotland. This has created many jobs and changed the lives of many Highlanders. The traditional industries of The Lowlands were coal-mining, ship-building and steel making. These industries have now almost disappeared. New industries include electronics, chemicals and light engineering.

### FAMOUS SCOTS
Scotland has produced many famous people, chiefly engineers and inventors. James Watt, the inventor of the steam engine, was Scottish. The unit of electrical power was named after him. Thomas Telford, another engineer, built the first iron bridge in the world in 1779. In 1926 another Scot, James Logie Baird, invented television. The Scottish doctor, Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928. For a small country, Scotland has had a big influence on the world.

activities.title: Active to Passive Voice
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the active sentence and rewrite it in the passive voice. Remember to use 'by' if the agent is important.
activities.compensates: Replaces the teacher-led review and correction of Workbook exercise 3.15A.

prompts.prompt: We must organize the race better.
prompts.explanation: The object 'the race' becomes the subject. We use the modal 'must' + 'be' + past participle 'organized'.
correct_responses: The race must be organized better.

prompts.prompt: They have discovered a lot of oil in the North Sea.
prompts.explanation: This is in the present perfect. The passive form is 'has/have been' + past participle. The agent 'they' is not important, so we can omit it.
correct_responses: A lot of oil has been discovered in the North Sea.

prompts.prompt: Telford built the first iron bridge.
prompts.explanation: This is in the past simple. The passive form is 'was/were' + past participle. The agent 'Telford' is important, so we include it with 'by'.
correct_responses: The first iron bridge was built by Telford.

prompts.explanation: The passive form for the past simple is 'was' + past participle 'discovered'. The agent 'Fleming' is important information.
This is in the present simple. The passive form is 'is/are' + past participle 'visited'.
correct_responses: Scotland is visited by thousands of tourists.

activities.title: Choosing the Right Tense
activities.instruction: Complete the sentences by filling in the blanks with the correct form of the verb in brackets. Use tenses like 'used to', 'will be able to', 'will have to', 'is going to', or 'is to'.

content.feedback: Great effort! You've successfully completed the sentences. Keep it up! 🚀

sentences.text: The race ___ every May, but it's been stopped. (take place)

blanks.hint: This happened in the past, but not anymore.

sentences.explanation: We use 'used to + infinitive' to talk about something that happened regularly in the past but doesn't happen now.

sentences.text: When the electronics factory opens next year, more women ___ get jobs. (can)
sentences.explanation: The future form of 'can' is 'will be able to'.

sentences.text: I'm too tired to do my homework now. I ___ it tomorrow. (must do)
sentences.explanation: The future form of 'must' is 'will have to'.

sentences.text: Great news! I've just heard that the Government ___ a new road to our village. (build)
sentences.explanation: We use 'going to + infinitive' to talk about future intentions.

sentences.text: The President ___ the new hospital tomorrow. (open)
sentences.explanation: We use 'be + to + infinitive' to talk about a certain future event in a formal way.

activities.title: Adding Information with Relative Clauses
activities.instruction: Combine the two sentences into one using a non-defining relative clause with 'who' or 'which'. Don't forget the commas!
activities.compensates: Replaces the teacher-led explanation and practice of non-defining relative clauses (WB 3.15C).

prompts.prompt: My father has bought a new car. He works in the capital.
prompts.explanation: Use 'who' for people. The extra information 'who works in the capital' is placed inside commas after 'My father'.
correct_responses: My father, who works in the capital, has bought a new car.

prompts.prompt: The Tower of London is the oldest building in London. It stands on the banks of The Thames.
prompts.explanation: Use 'which' for things. The extra information is placed inside commas.
correct_responses: The Tower of London, which stands on the banks of The Thames, is the oldest building in London.

prompts.prompt: The black stork comes from Africa. It lives in Yemen for half the year.
prompts.explanation: Use 'which' for animals/things. The relative clause adds extra, non-essential information.
correct_responses: The black stork, which lives in Yemen for half the year, comes from Africa.

prompts.prompt: In the reign of Queen Arwa, many new mosques were built. She died in 1138 at the age of 92.
prompts.explanation: Use 'who' for people. The clause 'who died in 1138 at the age of 92' gives extra information about Queen Arwa.
correct_responses: In the reign of Queen Arwa, who died in 1138 at the age of 92, many new mosques were built.
